title: The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis

jokes.text: Mac reveals he's been running the bar on a gasoline generator for a week because he thought it would be cheaper than electricity
jokes.setup: The gang is complaining about energy costs and scaling back
jokes.punchline: Mac has been running the bar on a gasoline generator — which is orders of magnitude more expensive than electricity — thinking he was saving money
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP cold open — the gang is trying to solve a problem they themselves created through stupidity. Mac's confident, week-long commitment to this terrible financial decision perfectly sets up the episode's theme of catastrophic overconfidence. Strong character integration because it's exactly the kind of self-defeating logic Mac would apply.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'You're the looks.' Mac: 'Hey of course I'm the looks, but I was seeing myself as the brains and the looks.' Mac's indignant acceptance that yes, he is the looks
jokes.setup: Mac pushes back on not being the brains of the operation
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately and completely accepts 'looks' as his role with zero pushback — only objecting that he thought he was BOTH looks AND brains
jokes.explanation: This is sharp character comedy — Mac's vanity is so thoroughly established that he doesn't even bother fighting the 'looks' label, only the implication that he COULDN'T be both. The beat perfectly encapsulates both Mac's vanity and his fundamental acceptance of a shallow hierarchy. High character integration: this exact response could only come from Mac.

jokes.text: Charlie reacts to being called 'the wild card' with pure delight: 'Oh! That's awesome.' / 'Yeah! Yeah, that's the classic setup.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is breaking down the crew dynamic: looks, brains, wild card
jokes.punchline: Charlie, who has just been assigned the least prestigious and most chaotic role, is THRILLED — he sees it as a badge of honor
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration — Charlie's enthusiasm for being labeled the unhinged, unpredictable element of the group is perfect. His joy at this dubious distinction reveals his entire psychology in two words. The 'classic setup' follow-up from Dennis treating pop-cultural archetypes as sacred organizational theory compounds the absurdity beautifully.

jokes.text: Dennis earnestly cites The A-Team, Scooby-Doo, and Ghostbusters as historical precedents for the Brains/Looks/Wild Card framework
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining the 'classic dynamic' of their crew as if it's established organizational theory
jokes.punchline: His examples of 'every great crew in history' are entirely fictional pop-culture teams, delivered with the gravity of a business consultant
jokes.explanation: Dennis treating Scooby-Doo as a legitimate organizational model with the same weight as a business framework is a great absurdist beat. The escalating list (A-Team → Scooby-Doo → Ghostbusters) works because each one is simultaneously more ridiculous and more enthusiastically co-signed by the gang. Strong character work: Dennis's delusion about his own intelligence is on full display.

jokes.text: 'We're getting plowed in the ass by the oil companies... with their ten-gallon hats and their rotten, ass-plowing hearts.'
jokes.setup: Dennis pivots to the matter at hand — the gas crisis
jokes.punchline: His description of corporate exploitation uses aggressive sexual metaphor with oddly specific details ('ten-gallon hats,' 'rotten, ass-plowing hearts'), delivered as serious political analysis
jokes.explanation: The 'ass-plowing' metaphor is a reliable IASIP crude-but-earnest construction. The addition of 'ten-gallon hats' as the specific grievance-marker is a funny detail. Works as character comedy — Dennis expressing political grievance through sexual violence metaphor is very on-brand — but it's not particularly original for the show.

jokes.text: 'It involves pulling up our bootstraps, oiling up a couple of asses and doing a little plowing of our own. Pow!'
jokes.setup: Dennis promises a plan that involves 'pulling up bootstraps' — classic entrepreneurial language
jokes.punchline: The metaphor immediately devolves back into ass-plowing imagery, with the triumphant 'Pow!' making it sound like a business pitch
jokes.explanation: A quick callback that escalates the ass-plowing metaphor by having Dennis adopt it as their own strategy. The 'Pow!' punctuation is a nice touch — his genuine enthusiasm for what sounds like a sexual proposition. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Not gay sex.' — Dennis clarifying his plan after everyone clearly interpreted the ass-plowing pitch as gay sex
jokes.setup: Dennis's pitch was explicitly about 'oiling up asses' and 'plowing'
jokes.punchline: His clarification is delivered as though the sexual interpretation was an obvious misunderstanding, when it was the only reasonable reading
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words that land the laugh entirely through the implied visual of everyone's confused/concerned faces. Mac's 'Okay, 'cause that's what it sounded like' follow-up earns additional points. The deadpan clarification structure is well-executed. High quotability because it's so contextually funny out of context.

jokes.text: Mac's 'big-breasted women chart' as a persuasion tool for the bank loan officer
jokes.setup: Dennis is laying out the seemingly reasonable plan to get a bank loan to speculate on gasoline
jokes.punchline: Mac mentions he'll supplement the pitch with a chart featuring 'big-breasted women' as a tiebreaker if the loan officer isn't going for it
jokes.explanation: The setup here is subtle — Mac treats the breasted-women chart as a legitimate business backup plan, and Dennis's 'Yeah, I'm sure it will' is perfect deadpan validation. This seeds the later payoff when the loan officer turns out to be a woman. Good plant-and-payoff structure across the episode.

jokes.text: Charlie complaining that he 'doesn't have anything to do' in the plan — his role is to 'sit there looking crazy and capable of anything'
jokes.setup: Charlie feels left out of the bank loan plan
jokes.punchline: His assigned role is to do absolutely nothing — just exist menacingly as psychological pressure
jokes.explanation: The gap between Charlie's concern about not having a job and the job he's assigned (literally just being himself) is a good joke. It also sets up the wild card face bit that follows. Good character integration — only Charlie could have this role.

jokes.text: Charlie demonstrates his 'wild card face' and it looks terrible — Mac and Dennis react with confusion and horror
jokes.setup: Charlie is asked to demonstrate his intimidating 'wild card face' for the bank meeting
jokes.punchline: The face he makes is apparently so bad/wrong that Mac says 'That's terrible' and Dennis asks 'What message are you trying to send with that?' — it reads as though Charlie looks like he needs to use the bathroom
jokes.explanation: Strong visual comedy inferred from dialogue — we can't see the face but Mac's 'That's terrible' and Dennis's 'you want him to think you're going to take a dump?' tell us everything. Charlie's earnest attempts to refine the face ('What if it's more like...') and the gang's escalating horror is very funny. Rewatch bonus because knowing what the face looks like on screen makes the transcript lines funnier in retrospect.

jokes.text: 'And you want him to think that you're going to take a dump or...?'
jokes.setup: Charlie has attempted a second, improved wild card face
jokes.punchline: Mac's reading of the face is that it looks like Charlie needs to defecate — delivered with the clinical detachment of a helpful note
jokes.explanation: The specific, mundane reading ('take a dump') is funnier than a more dramatic interpretation would be. Mac's matter-of-fact delivery of this feedback is well-calibrated. Good economy — the trailing 'or...' implies there might be an even worse interpretation.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I'd better look in a mirror 'cause I don't know what I'm doing and what it looks like feel like two different things.'
jokes.setup: Charlie's wild card faces keep being misread
jokes.punchline: Charlie's earnest, slightly broken articulation of the gap between his intention and execution is somehow both insightful and deeply stupid
jokes.explanation: Charlie's grammar is slightly broken ('what it looks like feel like') in a way that's authentically Charlie — it sounds like something a not-quite-literate person would say while still making perfect sense. The sincerity of his self-diagnosis is funny. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Dennis dismissing the van as 'not a rape van, it's a spy van' while Frank insists it looks very much like a rape van
jokes.setup: Frank has acquired a van for surveillance purposes
jokes.punchline: Dennis's rebranding attempt ('spy van') fails immediately because Frank agrees it looks like a rape van
jokes.explanation: The 'rape van' gag is a recurring IASIP element. The specific comic beat here is Dennis attempting a semantic reframe that immediately fails. Functional but not especially novel for the show.

jokes.text: Dee reveals her plan was to 'eliminate everybody else and be the only surviving heir' — casually admitting she planned to kill her entire family for inheritance money
jokes.setup: Dee is explaining why she needs help getting back the family money from Bruce Mathis
jokes.punchline: Her 'plan' involved murdering all other heirs — revealed with the same matter-of-fact tone as someone describing a grocery list, followed immediately by '...so help.'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The escalating reveal — 'I had a plan. I was going to eliminate everybody else and be the only surviving heir, so... help.' — is beautifully structured. The pivot on 'so... help' is pitch-perfect, treating the murder plot as merely a contextual detail before her actual ask. It's dark, it's character-specific (Dee's sociopathy), and 'so... help' is immediately quotable. The casualness of the admission is what makes it work.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'So when you say eliminate, you mean you were going to kill me?' Dee: 'I don't know. No, yes, maybe I was...'
jokes.setup: Dennis processes Dee's murder-for-inheritance admission
jokes.punchline: Dee's answer to whether she was going to kill Dennis is 'I don't know. No, yes, maybe I was going to; maybe I wasn't. The point is moot now.'
jokes.explanation: The cascading 'I don't know. No, yes, maybe' is very funny — Dee hasn't even decided if she was going to kill her own brother, and 'The point is moot now' treats his potential murder as a mere scheduling conflict. Strong follow-through on the previous beat.

jokes.text: Dennis's escalating refusals: 'Pass.' / 'Super-pass, berpass...' / 'I pass! I pass! Because you were planning on killing me.'
jokes.setup: Dee is asking Dennis to help with the Bruce Mathis money situation despite having just admitted she planned to kill him
jokes.punchline: Dennis invents increasingly emphatic non-words ('super-pass, berpass') to refuse, then collapses into the most reasonable possible objection
jokes.explanation: 'Super-pass, berpass' is a good improvised-escalation gag — Dennis inventing vocabulary for the intensity of his refusal. The return to 'because you were planning on killing me' as the calm, final explanation is well-structured.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Oh, my God, I feel like you're really focused on one tiny part of what I'm trying to talk about here.' Dennis: 'It's a very big part...'
jokes.setup: Dennis won't help Dee because she was planning to kill him
jokes.punchline: Dee characterizes 'you were going to murder me' as a 'tiny part' of the conversation Dennis is unfairly fixating on — with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Dee treating her fratricide plan as a minor conversational tangent Dennis is rudely derailing is excellent character comedy. 'It's just a couple of words' is a great follow-up — minimizing murder as a matter of word count. Strong character integration: Dee's oblivious sociopathy is perfectly on display.

jokes.text: 'Go away. I'm trying to draw breasts and pretty women.'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to get the gang's attention about Bruce Mathis while Mac is working on his 'chart'
jokes.punchline: Mac dismisses the life-or-death money situation to focus on drawing women with breasts — delivered as if this is a completely reasonable prioritization
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the earlier 'chart' plant, now revealed as Mac sitting there earnestly drawing busty women while Dee is urgently trying to discuss murder and money. The payoff on the chart setup is satisfying. 'I'm trying to draw breasts and pretty women' is quotable in its specificity.

jokes.text: Mac's dramatic 'Wait for it...' pause before answering the loan officer's question about why they want the loan — the answer is just 'Gasoline.'
jokes.setup: The loan officer asks what the loan is for — Mac builds theatrical suspense with 'Wait for it...'
jokes.punchline: The answer is simply 'Gasoline.' — completely anti-climactic and mundane despite the theatrical buildup
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP anti-climax. The structure is perfect: theatrical pause, expectation of something impressive, then the most mundane possible answer. Dennis's 'Don't rush him' adding to the buildup, then the loan officer's baffled 'Excuse me' completing the beat. Tight construction, good economy — the gap between performance and content is the joke.

jokes.text: Mac's loan pitch in its entirety: 'You give us a shitload of money. We buy a shitload of gasoline. We wait 12 months, we sell the gasoline and make a shitload of profit.'
jokes.setup: Mac is delivering the formal business pitch to a bank loan officer
jokes.punchline: The entire pitch consists of the word 'shitload' three times and no actual business logic or numbers beyond '12 months'
jokes.explanation: The triple 'shitload' construction is effective. The rhythm — shitload/shitload/shitload — has an almost musical quality that makes it funnier than it has any right to be. Mac's total confidence in this as a complete business pitch is essential to the joke working.

jokes.text: 'You give us a shitload of money. We buy a shitload of gasoline. We wait 12 months, we sell the gasoline and make a shitload of profit.'
jokes.setup: Mac is presenting his business plan to a bank loan officer
jokes.punchline: The 'business plan' is three sentences with no financial detail, three uses of 'shitload,' and delivered with the confidence of a TED talk
jokes.explanation: The triple 'shitload' is rhythmically perfect — it's not random, it creates a staccato business-speak parody. The confidence of delivery elevates what could be a cheap profanity gag into genuine character comedy. Very quotable as a standalone.

jokes.text: The gang discovers the loan officer is a woman after the entire pitch was built around impressing a man with a breasted-women chart
jokes.setup: Mac's backup plan was a chart featuring busty women to appeal to a male loan officer
jokes.punchline: The loan officer is a woman, and the chart is now completely counterproductive
jokes.explanation: Well-executed plant and payoff — the breasted women chart is set up earlier and pays off here. The loan officer's reaction to being shown a graph with women with 'heaving breasts' on it, presented by men who explain 'we sort of thought we'd be speaking to a man today,' is a good cringe beat.

jokes.text: Mac reveals the graph: 'And what are those?' / 'These are gorgeous women with heaving breasts.' / 'Why?' / 'Well, to be perfectly honest, we sort of thought we'd be speaking to a man today'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis present a business graph to the female loan officer; the graph contains unrelated drawings of busty women
jokes.punchline: The 'strategy' of including pin-up art in a bank loan presentation, explained with complete sincerity as a miscalculation about the audience's gender, escalates the cringe perfectly
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best cringe sequences. The beat where the loan officer asks 'Why?' and Mac answers 'we sort of thought we'd be speaking to a man' is an IASIP-caliber cringe moment — the characters aren't embarrassed, the audience is embarrassed for them. The setup (Dennis drawing breasts for the presentation) pays off perfectly here.

jokes.text: Mac to the female loan officer: 'Is there any way we can talk to your boss because I think he would understand more better?'
jokes.setup: The loan officer is a woman, the graph with busty women has not worked, and she's about to reject them
jokes.punchline: Mac asks to speak to 'her boss' (assumed to be male) and uses 'more better' — a double negative that reveals his lack of education as much as his sexism
jokes.explanation: 'More better' is a subtle but effective touch — Mac's condescension toward the loan officer is undercut by his own grammatical failure. The loan officer's response ('My boss is a woman') perfectly completes the beat. 'Now this is a strange bank' — Dennis's reaction to a bank with two female supervisors — is a good follow-up.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Now, this is a strange bank.' — reacting to being told the boss is also a woman
jokes.setup: Mac assumed the boss would be a man; the loan officer reveals her boss is also a woman
jokes.punchline: Dennis's response treats a bank with female management as an inexplicable anomaly
jokes.explanation: Good economy — four words that nail Dennis's oblivious sexism. The deadpan delivery makes it land better than a bigger reaction would. Slightly less sharp than some of the episode's better one-liners.

jokes.text: Charlie interrupting Dennis's seduction by offering 'Or how about we all go in the back and have great sex?' as a 'wild card'
jokes.setup: Dennis has his shirt off and is attempting to seduce the loan officer to get the loan
jokes.punchline: Charlie, trying to 'pull a wild card,' escalates to a group sex proposal — which is somehow even less subtle than Dennis's already-disastrous approach
jokes.explanation: The 'wild card' role paying off disastrously is a good structural beat. Charlie misunderstanding what a wild card does and immediately nuking Dennis's (already terrible) seduction attempt by going to 'we all have great sex' is very Charlie.

jokes.text: Mac: 'You can't pull the wild card when I already have my shirt off, that should be a rule.' Dennis: 'Yes, that's a rule.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has derailed Dennis's shirtless seduction attempt
jokes.punchline: Mac invents an on-the-spot rule about wild card timing relative to shirt removal, and Dennis ratifies it immediately as official gang policy
jokes.explanation: The speed with which Dennis ratifies Mac's absurd rule as official procedure is funny. The rule itself — that the wild card cannot interfere once someone has removed their shirt — is the kind of internal gang logic that makes IASIP great. It treats a seduction disaster as a matter requiring procedural clarification.

jokes.text: The situation devolves into all three men (Dennis, Mac, Charlie) simultaneously offering to have sex with the loan officer while arguing about whose turn it is
jokes.setup: Dennis's seduction has spiraled into chaos with Charlie and Mac both trying to participate
jokes.punchline: The loan officer is asked 'Which one of us do you want to take you in the back and bang you?' — by a committee of three increasingly desperate men
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the bank scene pays off here — three grown men competing for the right to sexually proposition a loan officer who has already rejected their business pitch. The cringe is well-earned and the visual of them arguing amongst themselves while she watches is strong. Slightly bloated by this point in the scene.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I waterboarded some guy. Told me everything.' Dee: 'You tortured somebody?'
jokes.setup: Dee asks Frank where he got his 'intel' about Bruce Mathis's location
jokes.punchline: Frank casually reveals he tortured someone for information — presented as a reasonable intelligence-gathering method
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Frank's matter-of-fact 'I waterboarded some guy' — delivered as a perfectly normal answer to 'where'd you get your intel?' — is the kind of casually monstrous Frank moment the show does best. The deadpan 'Told me everything' implies total satisfaction with the results. High character integration: Frank's willingness to do completely illegal, violent things for mundane goals is his defining trait. 'Big time' as a follow-up to 'You tortured somebody?' is the perfect punctuation.

jokes.text: The van has tinted windows on the INSIDE — Frank can't see out of his own surveillance vehicle
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee are in the surveillance van trying to spot Bruce Mathis
jokes.punchline: Frank tinted the inside of the windows so nobody could see in — meaning they also can't see out. 'I might've overdone it a little bit.'
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly stupid visual gag. Frank's solution to privacy concerns — tinting the INSIDE of the windows — reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of how windows work, delivered with complete confidence. 'I might've overdone it a little bit' is the perfect understatement from someone who didn't just 'overdo it' but got the entire concept backwards. Strong originality: the logical failure here is specific and funny, not generic stupidity.

jokes.text: The van's gas pedal gets stuck and Frank has to 'wiggle it' — 'Wiggle it. Wiggle it. That's it.' — to get the van moving, while trying to tail someone
jokes.setup: Frank spots Bruce Mathis and urgently tries to follow him in the van
jokes.punchline: The van's gas pedal is stuck and requires manual wiggling before it will respond, destroying any chance of a smooth tail
jokes.explanation: Functional slapstick — the broken van gag works as physical comedy and sets up later plot beats (the pedal becomes plot-relevant again). Not particularly original but well-integrated into the episode's mechanics.

jokes.text: Mac rams into someone's car five times trying to get the van unstuck — 'Mac rammed into some dude's car, like, five times. It was amazing.'
jokes.setup: The van has a stuck gas pedal
jokes.punchline: Mac's solution to the mechanical problem is to ram another car five times; this is later reported with the energy of someone recounting a cool story
jokes.explanation: The 'five times' detail and 'it was amazing' framing are good — the destruction is reported as impressive rather than embarrassing. The 'Hey, assholes' from the other driver and the cut away is clean. The gag is funnier in the callback ('five times, it was amazing') than in the moment.

jokes.text: Mac can't believe Dee keeps her life savings in her sock drawer — 'That's a dumb place to hide it.' Dennis: 'She's an investor now. She'll thank us later.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are using Dee's savings (taken without her knowledge) to fund their gasoline scheme
jokes.punchline: Dennis frames stealing Dee's money as doing her a favor — she's now an 'investor' in a scheme she doesn't know about
jokes.explanation: Dennis's rationalization of theft as investment advising is good character work. 'She'll thank us later' is a classic self-serving justification. The sock drawer detail grounds the joke with a specific visual.

jokes.text: Charlie complaining about the Ghostbusters comparison: 'The Ghostbusters would never do something like that to each other.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is upset that Mac and Dennis took their shirts off during the bank seduction scene, feeling betrayed
jokes.punchline: He invokes the Ghostbusters — their sacred organizational model — as a moral standard the gang has failed to meet
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the Ghostbusters were invoked as a model of organizational excellence, and now Charlie is citing them as a moral authority. The idea that the Ghostbusters' inter-team loyalty is a standard the gang should aspire to is both funny and sad.

jokes.text: Gas station attendant confronting Mac: 'No trash cans, only cars.' Mac's reaction: 'Whoa, cool your jets, guy. We paid for this gas.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to fill containers with gasoline at a gas station
jokes.punchline: The attendant is so accustomed to people filling trash cans with gas that he has a specific policy: 'No trash cans, only cars' — implying this is a recurring enough problem to require a standing rule
jokes.explanation: The gas station attendant having a specific 'no trash cans' policy implies a whole world of disasters that have come before. 'Only cars' as the contrast class is funny — the bar for acceptable gas containers is just 'cars.' Good economy.

jokes.text: Charlie threatening to 'blow this place to kingdom come' as his wild card response to the gas station conflict
jokes.setup: The gas station attendant won't let them fill trash cans; Dennis tells Charlie to do 'his thing'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's 'thing' is threatening to blow up the entire gas station — surrounded by gasoline barrels
jokes.explanation: Perfect wild card execution — Charlie immediately escalates to maximum threat. Dennis's 'Not that, not that. Jesus Christ, Charlie' response confirms that this is both unpredictable and completely useless as a negotiating tactic. The irony of threatening to blow up the thing they're trying to buy is well-observed.

jokes.text: Mac reveals he's been transporting gasoline by mouth-siphoning it and has 'swallowed a good deal of it'
jokes.setup: The gang is discussing how they're losing money on the gasoline scheme
jokes.punchline: Mac mentions as a footnote that he's been ingesting gasoline while siphoning it, treating it as a minor logistical note rather than a medical emergency
jokes.explanation: 'I have swallowed a good deal of it. It's just a damn waste.' — the concern here is entirely about wasted product, not personal poisoning. Mac treating his own gasoline consumption as a business inefficiency rather than a health crisis is excellent dark comedy and very IASIP.

jokes.text: Mac's gas station negotiation: 'You can't do it or you won't do it?' — Gas attendant: 'Both.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to return gasoline to a gas station for a refund
jokes.punchline: The attendant's 'Both' — combining ability and willingness into a single refusal — is the perfect one-word escalation of Mac's rhetorical trap
jokes.explanation: 'Both' is a great one-word punchline. Mac's attempt to find a legal/rhetorical loophole in 'can't vs. won't' is immediately and definitively shut down. The economy here is excellent.

jokes.text: Mac's business threat: 'You're about to experience the hard knocks of a free market, bitch. Get ready to feel it where it hurts. Your dick.' Dennis: 'No, no, not his dick. His wallet.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to intimidate the gas station owner with market forces
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'feel it where it hurts' naturally leads him to 'your dick,' which Dennis has to redirect to the actual financial threat
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Mac's business threat escalates perfectly to 'your dick' — his mind going to physical violence/humiliation rather than financial consequence. Dennis's patient correction ('No, no, not his dick. His wallet. Your wallet.') and the attendant's silent confusion is excellent. High quotability: 'Free market, bitch' into 'your dick' is the kind of line that gets clipped. Strong character integration: Mac's combination of aggression and financial illiteracy is perfectly on display.

jokes.text: Frank plants a baby monitor in Bruce Mathis's apartment as a 'bug'
jokes.setup: Frank is planting surveillance equipment in Bruce's apartment
jokes.punchline: The 'bug' Frank has acquired is a baby monitor — not a listening device — which he defends with 'A lot of people are bugging their babies these days'
jokes.explanation: Frank's earnest defense of using a baby monitor as surveillance equipment — 'A lot of people are bugging their babies these days. I guess babies can't be trusted.' — is a great absurdist beat. The logic is completely wrong (baby monitors transmit TO the parent, not FROM the subject) but Frank delivers it with total confidence. Sets up the later payoff when the baby monitor broadcasts the golf game.

jokes.text: Frank plants a baby monitor as a 'bug': 'That's a baby monitor, Frank.' / 'Yeah?' / 'A lot of people are bugging their babies these days. I guess babies can't be trusted.'
jokes.setup: Frank reveals his surveillance device is a baby monitor
jokes.punchline: When corrected, Frank defends it by pivoting to a theory that surveilling babies is common practice — 'babies can't be trusted' — delivered as if it's a known sociological fact
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Babies can't be trusted' is an absurdist non-sequitur delivered as serious analysis — Frank deflects from the absurdity of his gadget choice by attacking babies' trustworthiness. It's a perfect Frank line: paranoid, delusional, completely committed. Extremely quotable and endlessly recontextualizable.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Maybe Bruce is banging dudes.' Dee: 'Why would that be shady?' Frank: 'Maybe the dudes are babies.'
jokes.setup: Dee asks what Frank expects to find in Bruce's apartment
jokes.punchline: Frank's escalation from 'banging dudes' (not shady) to 'maybe the dudes are babies' (extremely shady) is a classic IASIP dark escalation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The two-step structure is perfect: Dee correctly identifies that 'banging dudes' is not shady (a progressive note), which prompts Frank to escalate immediately to baby sexual abuse as the alternative hypothesis. The structure — normal → addressed → catastrophic escalation — is tightly constructed. 'Maybe the dudes are babies' lands like a bomb. Frank's total seriousness amplifies the horror-comedy. High quotability, strong economy.

jokes.text: Frank confronting Dee: 'Were you planning on offing me and then offing Dennis also?' — mid-mission
jokes.setup: Frank has heard about Dee's murder-for-inheritance plan from earlier in the episode
jokes.punchline: Frank interrupts active surveillance to process his potential murder mid-mission, treating it as urgent enough to address right now but also confused enough about the details to need clarification
jokes.explanation: A callback to Dee's murder plan. The timing — mid-mission, mid-apartment break-in — is funny. Frank's specific concern about the ORDER of murders ('and then offing Dennis also?') implies he's more concerned about the sequencing than the act itself. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dee defuses the 'did you plan to murder me' question by handing Frank the baby monitor and offering to hide it — instantly ending the conversation
jokes.setup: Frank keeps pushing Dee about whether she was going to kill him; Dee can't escape the question
jokes.punchline: Dee's solution is to redirect Frank with a task — 'Give me the baby monitor, I'll hide it for you' — and the murder question is immediately forgotten
jokes.explanation: The evasion works as a character beat — Dee is clever enough to redirect Frank's suspicion with a task. But the joke is more functional than exceptional. The humor is in how easily Frank is distracted.

jokes.text: 'Capitalism at work.' — Dennis's narration as Mac uses Mac's competitor-sign scheme
jokes.setup: The gang decides to undercut the gas station by posting lower prices on their own sign
jokes.punchline: Dennis narrates their petty competitive sabotage as 'Capitalism at work' — using the language of free market principles to describe what is basically vandalism
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'Capitalism at work' as a proud declaration and the actual petty action being narrated is a decent ironic beat. Functional but not one of the episode's highlights.

jokes.text: Mac: 'How exactly are you planning on counting a liquid?'
jokes.setup: Charlie explains his plan to 'count' how much gas goes into each car with a funnel
jokes.punchline: Mac's question reveals Charlie planned to literally count individual units of a liquid — the question itself exposes the absurdity without over-explaining it
jokes.explanation: Clean, efficient comedy. The question does all the work without spelling out the punchline — the audience fills in Charlie's mental image of counting liquid drops. Good economy.

jokes.text: Charlie proposes 'blowing fireballs' at passing cars to attract customers to their roadside gasoline stand
jokes.setup: The gang needs to attract customers to their illegal roadside gas stand
jokes.punchline: Charlie's marketing proposal is to blow fire from his mouth to get attention — which, to be fair, would work, but is catastrophically dangerous surrounded by barrels of gasoline
jokes.explanation: Charlie proposing fire-breathing as a customer-attraction technique is excellent wild-card logic — it's crazy but internally consistent. Dennis's objection 'This is really unsafe, dude' vs. Charlie's 'Trust me, Dennis, I know what I'm doing' sets up the disaster perfectly.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Wow. Okay, wow, I take back everything I just said.' — after Charlie successfully blows a fireball
jokes.setup: Dennis has just told Charlie not to blow a fireball because it's unsafe
jokes.punchline: The fireball is apparently so impressive that Dennis immediately reverses his safety objections
jokes.explanation: Dennis's total reversal upon seeing something impressive — abandoning all principles when presented with cool-looking danger — is very on-brand. The 'I take back everything I just said' is funny because it immediately follows legitimate safety concerns.

jokes.text: Mac immediately decides he wants to do a bigger fireball — Charlie accidentally sets Mac's head on fire
jokes.setup: Emboldened by Charlie's successful fireball, Mac wants to do an even bigger one
jokes.punchline: Mac gets his head set on fire in the attempt — 'Oh, I did. I burned him.' delivered by Charlie with mild surprise
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'successful fireball' to 'burned head' is predictable but well-executed. The physical comedy lands visually. Charlie's 'Oh, I did. I burned him.' is delivered with the casual observation of someone who's just noticed a minor accident.

jokes.text: Mac's first aid after getting his head burned: a towel and duct tape. 'Do you have anything other than a towel and duct tape?' / 'Not really.'
jokes.setup: Mac's head has been set on fire
jokes.punchline: The only available first aid is a towel and duct tape — and this is treated as basically adequate; 'Not really' confirms these are the only options
jokes.explanation: The minimalism of 'Not really' as a full response to 'do you have anything other than a towel and duct tape for a head burn' is good. These characters are so accustomed to injury that this counts as adequate care.

jokes.text: Mac demoting Dennis from 'brains' to 'muscle' after the head-burn incident, citing 'we confused your bossiness with braininess'
jokes.setup: Dennis's plan has repeatedly failed; Mac takes over as 'both the brains and the looks'
jokes.punchline: 'What happened was, we confused your bossiness with braininess, and those two are very different things.' — delivered with genuine insight from Mac, whose own braininess is highly questionable
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'We confused your bossiness with braininess' is a sharp, quotable observation that works on multiple levels: (1) it's accurate — Dennis IS bossy but not smart, (2) Mac delivering this insight while himself being not at all brainy is deeply ironic, and (3) it perfectly subverts the earlier Brains/Looks/Wild Card framework. High quotability, strong economy, excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Mac's new brilliant plan: door-to-door gasoline salesmen
jokes.setup: Mac has taken over as 'both the brains and the looks' and unveils his plan
jokes.punchline: The plan is 'door-to-door gasoline salesmen' — a patently insane and illegal business model presented as a stroke of genius
jokes.explanation: The idea itself is funny — nobody has ever sold gasoline door-to-door and there are very good reasons for this. Dennis and Charlie's immediate enthusiasm ('Oh, my God, that's amazing') treating it as a genuine breakthrough compounds the absurdity.

jokes.text: Charlie insists on wearing disguises for the door-to-door gas scheme. Dennis: 'They already don't know who we are.' Charlie: 'You're not letting the wild card do his thing.'
jokes.setup: Charlie wants disguises for the door-to-door gas scheme
jokes.punchline: Dennis correctly points out that disguises are unnecessary since nobody knows them — Charlie responds that Dennis is suppressing his wild card instincts, implying that pointless disguises ARE the wild card
jokes.explanation: 'You're not letting the wild card do his thing' as a defense of pointless disguises is a good Charlie line — he's weaponizing the 'wild card' designation to justify any random impulse. The 'Is there any reason behind what you're doing?' / 'Wild card.' exchange is a good punchline.

jokes.text: The baby monitor Frank planted broadcasts Bruce watching golf for three hours — 'Stewart's up on his second shot on the fairway, hole 15...'
jokes.setup: Frank planted a baby monitor in Bruce's apartment to gather 'intel'
jokes.punchline: The monitor broadcasts three hours of golf commentary — Dee and Frank have been sitting outside listening to golf instead of gathering useful information
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff on the baby monitor plant. The setup (Frank plants a baby monitor thinking it's a bug) pays off perfectly when it broadcasts golf commentary — fulfilling the 'baby monitor transmits TO listener' function in the most useless possible way. 'I mean, how has he been sitting there watching golf for three hours?' is the right beat to end on. Great structural comedy.

jokes.text: Dee realizes it's a baby monitor, blows their cover: 'Oh, cut it off!' — Bruce becomes suspicious
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee are listening to Bruce's baby monitor broadcast
jokes.punchline: Dee loudly announces the baby monitor and panics — blowing their surveillance cover in the most obvious way possible
jokes.explanation: A functional escalation beat — the baby monitor reveal leads to Dee and Frank being discovered. Competent but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Frank accusing Dee: 'I bet you still hide your money in your sock drawer.' Dee's attempt to deny it is immediately transparent.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee are arguing after their cover is blown
jokes.punchline: Frank accuses Dee of hiding money in her sock drawer — which we already know is true (Mac and Dennis stole it earlier) — and Dee's denial is unconvincing
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the sock drawer detail — the audience knows the money is gone and Dee doesn't, which creates dramatic irony. The beat is more structural than funny, serving to remind us of the subplot.

jokes.text: Frank panics at seeing a Muslim man get into the van — 'Is that a Muslim guy? He's getting in my van.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee are fleeing from Bruce's building; Frank sees someone getting into his van
jokes.punchline: Frank's immediate conclusion — 'Muslim guy' + 'getting in my van' = terrorist confirmation — reveals his entire paranoid worldview; this is the man who was planting box cutters and fertilizer to frame a charitable donor
jokes.explanation: Frank's reflexive racial profiling is played as dark comedy — his suspicions are presented as obviously wrong (it's Mac and Dennis's doing) and his entire plot has been based on this same irrational premise. Good character integration but slightly uncomfortable territory handled with reasonable care given IASIP's typical approach.

jokes.text: Charlie in a full cowboy/oil man disguise — bolo tie, hat — insisting on a Southern accent for the door-to-door gas pitch
jokes.setup: The gang is doing door-to-door gasoline sales; Charlie wanted disguises
jokes.punchline: Charlie has gone full cowboy-oil man costume (bolo tie, hat) and insists they need Southern accents because 'we're oil men. We would have Southern accents.'
jokes.explanation: The payoff on Charlie's disguise obsession — he's gone full costume and has a character logic for why ('oil men have Southern accents'). The costume itself is a good visual gag. Dennis's refusal to do the accent while wearing the stupid costume anyway is a nice character beat.

jokes.text: Charlie interrupts Dennis's door pitch with: 'Hells, yeah! We want to feel you up, if'n you were so inclined as to let us.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is attempting to explain their legitimate gasoline delivery service
jokes.punchline: Charlie's wild card improvisation turns the pitch into what sounds like a sexual proposition, complete with folksy 'if'n you were so inclined'
jokes.explanation: 'We want to feel you up, if'n you were so inclined as to let us' is a great line — the incongruity of the ultra-polite 'if'n you were so inclined' attached to 'feel you up' is very funny. Charlie's character logic (the Southern oil man would naturally say this) makes it funnier. Dennis's futile 'Please, let me do the talking' is the right reactive beat.

jokes.text: Mac's pained attempt to regain control: 'Please, let me do the talking. Please, let me...' while Charlie continues threatening the homeowner
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to run a professional door-to-door sales pitch
jokes.punchline: Mac's increasingly helpless 'please let me do the talking' as Charlie spirals into sexual threats is the perfect straight-man disintegration
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — Mac's breakdown is satisfying but not novel. The humor is in the inevitability of Charlie's escalation rather than any specific line.

jokes.text: Charlie, still in character, warning them about police: 'Yep, you best get to stepping, because Johnny Law's a-coming.' — continuing in the Southern accent long after it's served any purpose
jokes.setup: The homeowner has called the cops on them
jokes.punchline: Charlie warns the gang about the police in full cowboy character, using 'Johnny Law' and 'best get to stepping' — the character has fully consumed him
jokes.explanation: Charlie remaining in character while alerting them to genuine danger is excellent. 'Johnny Law's a-coming' as a police warning is very quotable. Dennis's 'Now you're just talking like Foghorn Leghorn' is the right meta-commentary to end the bit.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Well, now you're just talking like Foghorn Leghorn!'
jokes.setup: Charlie has been doing a Southern accent that has escalated into broad cartoon territory
jokes.punchline: Dennis identifies the specific pop-culture register Charlie has accidentally landed in
jokes.explanation: The 'Foghorn Leghorn' comparison is perfect — it identifies exactly what Charlie's accent has become without over-explaining. Dennis naming the cartoon character both punctuates the joke and validates the audience's reading of the scene. Good economy.

jokes.text: Frank accuses Dee and the 'Muslim guy' (actually Mac and Dennis) of conspiring to rub him out — Dee breaks and admits 'anything you want to hear'
jokes.setup: Frank has cornered Dee and is demanding confessions
jokes.punchline: 'Okay, okay, I admit it!' / 'What do you admit?!' / 'I admit anything you want to hear!' — Dee's total capitulation is the joke, admitting to whatever Frank wants including things she hasn't done
jokes.explanation: The 'I admit anything you want to hear' beat is good — it both undermines waterboarding as an intelligence tool and reveals Dee's complete failure of resistance. Frank pressing for details ('admit that Bruce Mathis is a terrorist') and Dee immediately complying with absurd additions ('We get our information from the top, the top cave') is funny.

jokes.text: Dee under 'waterboarding' confesses: 'Yes, I work for him. We get our information from the top, the top cave.'
jokes.setup: Frank has demanded Dee confess to working for Bruce Mathis as a terrorist
jokes.punchline: Dee invents 'the top cave' as her terrorist headquarters — a completely nonsensical detail she's adding to satisfy Frank
jokes.explanation: 'The top cave' is a funny detail — Dee is making up spy-thriller nonsense to satisfy Frank, and 'top cave' has the right ring of someone improvising a terrorist lair. The specificity ('the top') is what makes it funny over just 'a cave.'

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis discover Frank is waterboarding Dee when they arrive at the bar
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis return to the bar; Dee has been asking for help
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to finding Frank waterboarding Dee is 'Frank's waterboarding Dee' delivered as a simple status update, not a crisis
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands well — Frank has escalated from waterboarding random people for intel to waterboarding his own family member. The casualness with which everyone reports and receives this information is good character work for the show.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Hey, Frank, by the way, we borrowed that pathetic rape van of yours; you got to get that gas pedal fixed, man. Mac rammed into some dude's car, like, five times. It was amazing.'
jokes.setup: Frank is waterboarding Dee; Mac arrives
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers his report on the van — including ramming someone's car five times — with the energy of someone sharing a cool story, completely ignoring the ongoing waterboarding
jokes.explanation: Good callback consolidation — Mac's pride in having rammed someone's car five times, delivered mid-torture scene, is very IASIP. 'It was amazing' as an evaluation of property destruction is characteristically Mac.

jokes.text: Frank: 'You guys took the van? I thought it was some Muslim guy.' — realizing his entire paranoid terror plot was caused by his own crew
jokes.setup: Frank had been convinced a 'Muslim guy' getting into his van was connected to a terrorist conspiracy against him
jokes.punchline: It was just Mac the whole time — Frank's entire paranoid spiral was self-generated
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural payoff — Frank's entire subplot (waterboarding Dee, plotting against Bruce) was triggered by seeing Mac get in his own van. The reveal deflates the whole paranoia arc neatly. 'Not really' as the confirmation is good economy.

jokes.text: Dennis realizing: 'Frank is the muscle.' — and the gang completing their team with Dee as 'the useless chick'
jokes.setup: Dennis has a sudden revelation about why things haven't been working
jokes.punchline: Frank is the muscle (he just waterboarded someone), and Dee's role is formalized as 'the useless chick' — to her obvious displeasure, and everyone else's enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff on the episode's central conceit. 'Frank is the muscle' — earned by watching Frank casually waterboard someone — completes the team. 'She's the useless chick' and the gang's synchronized 'Yeah!' is a perfect beat. The structure of the entire episode has been building to this, and it pays off with strong character specificity: Dee's role being 'useless' rather than nothing is both insulting and strangely validating.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I got Dee to admit to things she never did! Well, then it works.' — Dennis validating waterboarding because it successfully extracted false confessions
jokes.setup: Dennis asks if waterboarding 'really works' as an intelligence tool
jokes.punchline: Frank confirms it works — it got Dee to confess to things she NEVER DID — and Dennis treats this as a successful proof of concept
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest moments. The joke operates as genuine political satire — the most damning critique of torture (it produces false confessions) is treated as a FEATURE by Dennis ('Well, then it works'). The gap between what Dennis hears ('waterboarding works') and what was actually proven ('waterboarding produces false confessions') is a pointed, well-constructed joke. Strong originality because it's doing real satirical work while fitting perfectly into the show's dark comedy framework. High impact because the punchline lands on a real idea.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Wait. Brakes don't... Brakes don't work.' — in a van full of gasoline barrels
jokes.setup: The whole gang is in the van heading to Bruce Mathis's place
jokes.punchline: The brakes don't work — in a van loaded with flammable gasoline with five people inside
jokes.explanation: The 'wiggle it' callback escalates to brakes-out in a gasoline van. The beat sets up the episode's climax and pays off both the mechanical van gags from earlier.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Because I cut the brakes! Wild card, bitches!' — revealing he deliberately cut the brakes
jokes.setup: The gang is screaming that the brakes don't work
jokes.punchline: Charlie cut the brakes himself as a 'wild card' move — explaining it triumphantly mid-crisis
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the great IASIP moments. The entire episode has been building the 'wild card' concept: Charlie's role is to be unpredictable, to not explain himself, to do things 'with no reason.' 'Because I cut the brakes! Wild card, bitches!' is the perfect, catastrophic payoff on this — Charlie has fully internalized the concept and applied it to deliberately endangering everyone's lives as a performance of his role. The 'bitches!' punctuation, the revelation that this was INTENTIONAL, and the perfect character integration (only Charlie) make this exceptional. It's comparable to the 'Snip, snap!' anchor in its escalation-to-revelation structure. Near-maximum scores are warranted.

jokes.text: The runaway gasoline van crashes into the golf course — cutting to a golfer mid-commentary ('Mastersfield steps up to the tee, eight strokes behind the leader. Hole number 17, 338 yards, dogleg left.')
jokes.setup: The van with no brakes is careening out of control; we've heard golf commentary before (the baby monitor)
jokes.punchline: The crash lands on a golf course — connecting the random golf commentary from Frank's baby monitor subplot to the main plot's catastrophic conclusion
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural callback — the golf commentary Frank had to sit through for three hours via baby monitor is now the setting of the episode's climactic disaster. The connection between the two subplots is elegant and rewarding on rewatch. The golf announcer's commentary ('dogleg left') playing over a crashing gasoline van is a perfect tonal contrast.

jokes.text: Frank emerging from the crash: 'Ah, my van. Why is someone trying to ruin my life?! I didn't do anything to anybody, man! I love that car!'
jokes.setup: The van has just crashed on a golf course after Charlie cut the brakes
jokes.punchline: Frank's immediate response to the crash he is partly responsible for (his van, his stolen gas pedal, his insistence on the scheme) is to position himself as an innocent victim
jokes.explanation: 'Why is someone trying to ruin my life?! I didn't do anything to anybody, man!' — Frank's self-pity after a disaster largely of his group's making is classic. 'I love that car!' (about a van he called 'pathetic' earlier) is a nice reversal.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'That's, uh, that's not Bruce, is it?' — realizing the person they just crashed into on the golf course is not their target
jokes.setup: The gang has crashed their gasoline van on a golf course in pursuit of Bruce Mathis
jokes.punchline: The person at the crash site is confirmed to not be Bruce — the entire scheme, the crash, the gasoline, all for nothing
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-ending beat — the tentative 'That's, uh, that's not Bruce, is it?' followed by a simple 'No' confirms that everything was for nothing. Good economy in the understatement. The two-beat silence implied by the exchange is funnier than any big joke would be here.

jokes.text: The episode ends with the Ghostbusters theme playing — 'If there's something strange in your neighborhood, who you gonna call? Ghostbusters!'
jokes.setup: Throughout the episode, the gang has used the Ghostbusters as their organizational model
jokes.punchline: The episode closes on the Ghostbusters theme — the gang has once again failed to live up to their fictional heroes; the music punctuates the irony
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural button on the episode's central gag. The Ghostbusters theme playing over the gang's total failure — crashed van, golf course, wrong target, nothing accomplished — is a good tonal payoff. The irony of 'who you gonna call?' when the gang has demonstrated they cannot solve anything is well-earned.

tmdb_overview: Charlie, Mac, and Dennis formulate a plan to take advantage of the rising gas prices. By purchasing excess amounts now, they can sell it in the future and profit. As usual, things don't go as planned. Dee is also out to make money when she learns that Bruce is going to give the family fortune to a Muslim cultural center. She and Frank try to stop him and get the cash for themselves.
